To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) aphid fecundy is regulated by redox signaling that is mediated, in part, through the PP2A-dependent mitochondrial to nucleus signaling pathways; (2) the redox signaling pathway is triggered by moderate light; (3) high light triggers the JA pathway, which is not involved in aphid fecundty; (4) the JA pathway is triggered by high light.
aphid fecundy is regulated by cellular redx signalling that is mediated at least in part through PP2A dependent mitochondria to nucleus signalinng pathways.

aphid fecundy is decreased under moderate light in mutants deficient in either the PP2A catalytic subunit PP2A-C (pp2a-c), the PP2A regulatory subunit PP2Ac (pp2a-b'c), the PP2Ac isoform γ1 (pp2a-γ1) or the PP2A-B regulatory subunit isoform γ2 (pp2a-g'γ2).
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of redox signalling in regulating aphid fecundities in Arabidopsis and the potential role of specific molecular components in mediating these responses.
understanding how plants and aphids respond to light, and how these responses are regulated by redox signalling pathways.
the role of reactive oxygen species (ROS) in the interaction of insects and plants.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the redox status of a cell is a major determinant of the outcome of the interaction between plants and insects.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
redox signaling is mediated by PP2A and that this is important in determining plant responses to aphid attack.

aphid fecundities are reduced in cat2 and the double mutant cat2cad2, and the triple mutant clt1pad2cat2 under moderate light.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the redox signalling pathways regulating aphid fecundities in Arabidopsis mutants are differentially affected by moderate versus high irradiance, with high light enhancing aphid fecundites in all genotypes.
redox signaling pathways regulate plant responses to insects and that this is regulated by light and specific molecular components.
the redox signalling pathways that regulate plant-insect interactions are differentially regulated by the environment and are mediated through different molecular components.
